01 — SEA FREIGHT

Ocean freight, from first principles

Sea freight is booked as an import or an export movement, and the cargo either fills a whole container or shares one. These four terms frame every ocean shipment DSV handles.

FIS · FES · FCL · LCL
FIS

Freight Import Sea

Inbound ocean freight — cargo arriving into India by vessel, cleared through customs at a sea port or ICD and delivered to the consignee.

FES

Freight Export Sea

Outbound ocean freight — cargo shipped from India to overseas ports, documented with a Shipping Bill and a Bill of Lading.

FCL

Full Container Load

One customer uses a full container for their cargo. Booked and measured in TEU — a 20ft box is 1 TEU, a 40ft box is 2 TEU.

20ft = 1 TEU40ft = 2 TEU
LCL

Less Container Load

Cargo from multiple customers is combined in one container. Charged by volume in CBM, so measurement accuracy drives the rate.

Charged per CBMConsolidated
MEASUREMENT UNITS

TEU counts containers.
CBM measures cargo.

The training rule of thumb: 1 TEU = 25 CBM. TEU (Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit) describes container capacity for FCL; CBM (cubic metre) describes the actual volume of the cargo and is the rating unit for LCL.

CBMCubic metre
=
L × W × HLength × Width × Height

Try it — enter one piece's dimensions and the piece count to get total CBM, the TEU equivalent, the air volumetric weight and a stowage suggestion.

CBM CALCULATOR
9.60Total CBM
0.38TEU equivalent
1,600 kgAir volumetric wt.
Suggestion: under 13 CBM, LCL consolidation is usually the economical sea option.
EQUIPMENT

Five container types cover almost everything

The General Purpose box is the most-used container in the fleet. Specialised equipment — high cube, reefer, flat rack and tank — is matched to what the cargo demands.

GP — General Purpose

The everyday workhorse

Used for normal cargo — cartons, machinery, electronics and furniture. Available in 20ft and 40ft.

20ft40ftMost used
HC — High Cube

Extra height, more volume

Used for bulky or high-volume cargo that needs extra height beyond a standard box — the 40ft High Cube.

40ft HCBulky cargo
RF — Reefer

Temperature-controlled

Refrigerated container for frozen and temperature-controlled items, holding a set temperature across the voyage.

FrozenCold chain
FR — Flat Rack

Open frame for special cargo

No side walls or roof — built for machinery and special, out-of-gauge cargo loaded from the top or sides.

MachineryOut-of-gauge
TC — Tank Container

Liquids in bulk

A pressure-rated tank inside a container frame, used for liquids such as oil and other bulk fluids.

LiquidsOil
MATCHING RULE

Cargo first,
container second

Weight, dimensions, temperature and shape decide the equipment — never the other way round. Oversized or heavy pieces point to FR; anything frozen points to RF.

02 — DOCUMENTS & CARRIERS

The Bill of Lading runs on two levels

A Bill of Lading contains the shipment and cargo details. Every consolidated sea shipment carries two of them — one issued by the forwarder to the customer, one issued by the shipping line for the container.

Issued by the freight forwarder

HBL — House Bill of Lading

The forwarder's document, issued by DSV / the co-loader for the customer's own cargo.

  • Covers the individual customer's shipment
  • Shipper: the exporter · Consignee: the importer
  • The document the customer surrenders to claim cargo
VS
Issued by the shipping line

MBL — Master Bill of Lading

The carrier's document, issued by the shipping line for the shipment / container as a whole.

  • Covers the full container with the line
  • Shipper: the forwarder · Consignee: the forwarder's agent
  • Sits behind every HBL inside that container
Shipping line

Owns the vessel & the boxes

A shipping line owns or operates ships to transport cargo, and provides the vessel and container capacity the forwarder books against. DSV works with the major global lines:

Hapag-LloydMSCCMA CGMCOSCOONEOOCLHMMPIL
NVOCC

A carrier without ships

A Non-Vessel Operating Common Carrier acts like a carrier — issuing its own Bills of Lading and taking responsibility for the shipment — but does not operate ships or vessels itself. It buys space from shipping lines and resells it as a consolidated service.

Issues HBLNo own vesselsBuys line capacity
CUSTOMS CLEARANCE

Six documents clear the border

Customs clearance is the government's approval to import or export goods. These are the documents the training material lists for every clearance file.

01

Commercial Invoice

The commercial transaction — seller, buyer, goods description and value details.

02

Packing List

Package and cargo details — pieces, weights and dimensions, carton by carton.

03

Bill of Lading

The transport document evidencing the contract of carriage with the line.

04

Shipping Bill

The export document filed for goods leaving the country.

05

Bill of Entry

The import document filed for goods entering the country.

06

Customs Declaration

The formal declaration, together with the applicable duty and tax assessment.

03 — AIR FREIGHT

Air freight, built for speed

Air cargo moves as exports (FEA) and imports (FIA), loose or built up into airline ULDs, on passenger aircraft bellies and dedicated freighters alike.

FEA · FIA · LSE · ULD
FEA

Freight Export Air

Outbound air freight — cargo tendered to an airline in India and flown to the destination airport under a Master Air Waybill.

FIA

Freight Import Air

Inbound air freight — shipments arriving by air, notified to the consignee, customs-cleared and delivered.

LSE — Loose cargo

Handled piece by piece

Loose airfreight is handled as individual pieces rather than as a consolidated ULD shipment — typical for smaller, urgent consignments.

Aircraft types

PAX vs CAO

PAX — passenger flight: cargo travels in the belly of a passenger aircraft. CAO — Cargo Aircraft Only: a freighter operation, required for cargo not permitted on passenger aircraft.

Narrow body ≈ 80–100 kg / pieceWide body ≈ 1,000–2,000 kg / piece
ULD — UNIT LOAD DEVICE

Special containers & pallets that carry cargo inside the aircraft

A ULD keeps cargo secured, protected and shaped to the aircraft's fuselage — a closed container, or a flat pallet with the cargo secured under a net.

PMC

Aircraft pallet. Cargo is built up on the flat pallet base and secured with a net — the main-deck and lower-deck workhorse.

AKE

Aircraft container. A small closed container used in the lower deck, contoured to fit the belly hold.

Reference piece dimensions from the training material: 100 × 100 × 100 cm · 100 × 80 × 80 cm · up to 350 × 250 × 155 cm on wide-body equipment.

Main-deck loading at duskPMC pallet & AKE container staged on the apron

CARGO TYPES

Seven ways air cargo is classified

The IATA special-handling code on the AWB tells everyone in the chain exactly how a shipment must be treated — temperature, security, welfare or equipment.

General

General Cargo

Normal goods that need no special handling — clothing, electronics, machinery parts.

PIL — Pharmaceutical

Pharma & healthcare

Medicines and healthcare products, often temperature-controlled — vaccines, medicines, medical samples.

2–8°C15–25°CNon-temp
DG — Dangerous Goods

Regulated & restricted

Goods that can create a safety risk and require special regulations and handling — batteries, chemicals, flammable materials.

PER — Perishable

Fresh, on the clock

Goods that can spoil or lose quality quickly — fruits, vegetables, flowers, fresh food.

AVI — Live Animals

Traveling animals

Live animals transported under specific welfare and handling requirements — dogs, cats, livestock.

VAL — Valuable

High value, high security

High-value goods requiring additional security and handling controls — gold, jewellery, expensive electronics.

HEA — Heavy / Oversized

Too big for standard

Cargo too large or heavy for normal handling; may need special equipment or loading arrangements.

READ THE CODE

The AWB is the instruction sheet

PIL, PER, AVI, VAL, DG — the handling code travels with the shipment from booking to delivery.

04 — AWB & RATING

Two waybills, two ways to price

The air waybill connects the customer, the forwarder and the airline. The rate built on it is either a bare freight charge or an all-in price — the difference is the surcharges.

CustomerHouse shipment
→
HAWBHouse Air Waybill · issued by DSV
→
DSVFreight forwarder
→
MAWBMaster Air Waybill · airline document
→
AirlineMaster shipment movement
Rate only

NET-NET++

Quoted without any surcharges — the rate is the air freight charge alone. Surcharges are added on top at invoicing.

  • Air freight charge only
  • FSE, SSE & XCH billed separately
  • Compare carriers on a like-for-like base
VS
Everything included

ALL-IN

Air freight plus the applicable surcharges, all inside the one quoted rate — the number you see is the number you pay for carriage.

  • Freight + surcharges in one rate
  • Simpler customer quotation
  • No separate surcharge lines
Surcharges in the rate build

What NET-NET++ leaves out

FSE — Fuel Surcharge SSE — Security Surcharge XCH — X-Ray Screening

These three surcharges are listed in the training material and are the difference between a NET-NET++ quote and an ALL-IN quote.

Weight slabs

Heavier breaks cost less per kilo

+45 kg break — from 45 kg the per-kilo rate drops. Always check the break-even against the Normal rate.

Break-even check: (higher slab × its rate) ÷ lower slab rate — compare both rating options and apply the commercially better one.

06 — INCOTERMS® 2020

Who delivers, who pays, who carries the risk

Incoterms® are international trade terms that clarify the agreed responsibilities between seller and buyer for delivery, costs and risk. Eleven rules: seven for any mode of transport, four for sea and inland waterway only. Always read the rule together with the sales contract and the named place or port — risk transfer is not always at the same point as cost responsibility.

ANY MODE Any mode of transport — 7 rules

EXW

Ex Works

Goods made available at the seller's premises — the buyer takes it from there.

FCA

Free Carrier

Seller delivers the goods to the named carrier at the named place.

CPT

Carriage Paid To

Seller pays carriage to the named destination; risk transfers earlier, at carrier handover.

CIP

Carriage & Insurance Paid To

Seller pays carriage and arranges insurance; risk transfers at carrier handover.

DAP

Delivered At Place

Seller delivers to the named place; the buyer handles unloading and import.

DPU

Delivered At Place Unloaded

Seller delivers and unloads at the named destination.

DDP

Delivered Duty Paid

Seller takes responsibility for delivery and import clearance and duties, subject to the contract.

READ IT IN 3 QUESTIONS

1 · Delivery point — where does the seller deliver?
2 · Risk transfer — at what point does risk move?
3 · Costs & insurance — who pays which elements?

SEA ONLY Sea & inland waterway — 4 rules

FAS

Free Alongside Ship

Seller places the goods alongside the vessel at the port of shipment.

FOB

Free On Board

Seller loads the goods on board; risk transfers when the goods are on board.

CFR

Cost & Freight

Seller pays cost and freight to the destination port; risk transfers on board.

CIF

Cost, Insurance & Freight

Seller pays cost and freight and arranges insurance; risk transfers on board.
